content.text:
No, it isn't guaranteed safe without a prefix. The docs give you two mitigations:

- **Use the `prefix` option.** `@import "tailwindcss" prefix(tw);` namespaces the classes and the theme variables. The compiled output has `--tw-color-red-500` and `.tw\:text-red-500` (`src/docs/styling-with-utility-classes.mdx`, "Managing style conflicts › Using the prefix option", lines 992–1020). It keeps `rounded-lg` and the other built-ins, and the variables are namespaced again.
- **Only used variables are emitted by default.** The docs say "By default only used CSS variables will be generated in the final CSS output" (`src/docs/theme.mdx`, "Generating all CSS variables", lines 518–531). Unused built-in variables therefore don't ship, though any you use do. I didn't find a section on how this affects collisions with a user's own `--color-*` variables.

The prefix is the safer option for a library that ships CSS to other people's sites. The cost is that your users' markup needs the `tw:` class prefix (a different prefix name works too).

The compiled output has `--tw-color-red-500` and `.tw\:text-red-500` (`src/docs/styling-with-utility-classes.mdx`, "Managing style conflicts › Using the prefix option", lines 992–1020). It keeps `rounded-lg` and the other built-ins, and the variables are namespaced again.
- **Only used variables are emitted by default.** The docs say "By default only used CSS variables will be generated in the final CSS output" (`src/docs/theme.mdx`, "Generating all CSS variables", lines 518–531). Unused built-in variables therefore don't ship, though any you use do. I didn't find a section on how this affects collisions with a user's own `--color-*` variables.

The prefix is the safer option for a library that ships CSS to other people's sites. The cost is that your users' markup needs the `tw:` class prefix (a different prefix name works too).
